title: Ὄφις καὶ γαλῆ καὶ μύες
titleEn: The Snake, the Weasel and the Mice
part: The Snake, the Weasel and the Mice (Chambry 289)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 289. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄφις καὶ γαλῆ ἔν τινι οἰκίᾳ ἐμάχοντο.
sentences.tr: Ophis kai galē en tini oikiāi emachonto.
sentences.l: A snake and a weasel were fighting in a certain house.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ ἐνταῦθα μύες ἀεὶ καταναλισκόμενοι ὑπὸ ἀμφοτέρων, ὡς ἐθεάσαντο αὐτοὺς μαχομένους, ἐξῆλθον βαδίζοντες.
sentences.tr: Hoi de entautha myes aei katanaliskomenoi hypo amphoterōn, hōs etheasanto autous machomenous, exēlthon badizontes.
sentences.l: And the mice there, being always consumed by both of them, when they saw them fighting, came out walking.
sentences.i: The mice of the house, who were forever being eaten up by the pair of them, saw the two at their fight and came strolling out.
sentences.n: καταναλίσκω is to spend a thing right up, and of eating to devour to the last — the moral will bring the same root back in παρανάλωμα. In ἐξῆλθον βαδίζοντες the participle gives the manner: they walk out rather than scurry.

sentences.t: Ἰδόντες δὲ τοὺς μύας, τότε ἀφέντες τὴν πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς μάχην, ἐπ’ ἐκείνους ἐτράπησαν.
sentences.tr: Idontes de tous myas, tote aphentes tēn pros heautous machēn, ep’ ekeinous etrapēsan.
sentences.l: But having seen the mice, then, having dropped the battle against one another, they turned upon those.
sentences.i: But when they caught sight of the mice, they dropped the fight between themselves and turned on them.
sentences.n: Two aorist participles carrying the action to a single finite verb — the ordinary engine of these fables. πρὸς ἑαυτούς is the reflexive used reciprocally, 'against each other'. ἐτράπησαν is the aorist passive of τρέπω used intransitively, 'they turned'.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πόλεων οἱ ἐν ταῖς τῶν δημαγωγῶν στάσεσιν ἑαυτοὺς παρεισβάλλοντες λανθάνουσιν αὐτοὶ ἑκατέρων παρανάλωμα γινόμενοι.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai epi tōn poleōn hoi en tais tōn dēmagōgōn stasesin heautous pareisballontes lanthanousin autoi hekaterōn paranalōma ginomenoi.
sentences.l: So too in the case of cities, those who throw themselves in among the factions of the popular leaders escape their own notice becoming themselves the incidental waste of each of the two sides.
sentences.i: So too with cities: those who push themselves in among the quarrels of rival popular leaders are used up as waste by both sides, and never see it coming.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a supplementary participle works the reverse way from English — the participle carries the action and the verb says only that it went unnoticed (as at fable 217, likewise on cities). παρανάλωμα is what gets spent by the way, the incidental waste, and it is the same root as the mice's καταναλισκόμενοι in the story. στάσις is the standing word for party strife inside a city, and ἑκατέρων, 'of each of the two', keeps the two parties apart.
